facts.title: A CXL Memory Rack for Multi-Turn LLM Serving
facts.event_hint: HyMCache: CXL-hybrid memory rack for multi-turn LLM KV-cache serving
facts.problem: Multi-turn LLM serving requires TB-scale shared KV-cache capacity to reuse context across turns and sessions, but GPU HBM and host DRAM are too costly to scale to this level. Storage-backed tiers provide capacity but require software staging overhead. Pure DRAM-based CXL memory pools provide low latency but remain expensive at multi-TB scale.
facts.mechanism: HyMCache builds a remote memory rack using CXL-hybrid memory (CXL-HM), which combines small in-device DRAM with large SSD-backed capacity behind a CXL.mem interface. It exploits read-dominant, predictable, and append-only KV-cache access patterns with request-level prefix prefetching and opportunistic write buffering to stage latency-critical reads in device DRAM, enabling DRAM-scale efficiency at SSD-level cost.

evidence.claim: CXL-HM prototype costs $10.5K-$11.0K vs Distributed Mooncake DRAM tier at $30K-$40K
evidence.baseline: Distributed Mooncake 1TB DDR5 RDIMM DRAM tier
evidence.condition: FPGA-based CXL-HM prototype with Agilex 7 development board, 64 GB device-side DRAM, two Gen5 SSDs; Mooncake uses 1 TB DDR5 RDIMM
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 10: Cost estimates for remote-tier components

evidence.claim: HyMCache hit ratio reaches 74% vs Distributed Mooncake at 65% in Qwen2.5-32B multi-turn serving
evidence.condition: 4P-1D-1S setup, Qwen2.5-32B model, mooncake trace workload, Turn 7
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 9, Figure 8: Hit ratio comparison

evidence.claim: Distributed Mooncake achieves ~30% higher performance than HyMCache but at 3-4x cost
evidence.condition: Qwen2.5-32B serving, same remote tier setup with ConnectX-6 RNIC and two Gen5 SSDs; Mooncake E2E TTFT 22.0s vs HyMCache 27.4s
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 10: Performance comparison and cost discussion

evidence.claim: HyMCache uses 16x less DRAM than 1TB distributed-DRAM Mooncake at ~30% performance gap
evidence.condition: HyMCache CXL-HM with 64 GB device-side DRAM; Mooncake with 1 TB DDR5 RDIMM; abstract claim - detailed metrics in evaluation section

evidence.claim: NVMe-oF raw bandwidth 23 GB/s per node but drops to 6.5 GB/s with XFS filesystem overhead
evidence.value: 23 GB/s raw vs 6.5 GB/s with XFS
evidence.condition: ConnectX-6 RNIC, 200 Gbps network limit, Gen5 SSDs, XFS-mounted NVMe-oF volume
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 10: Software I/O path overhead discussion

facts.evaluation_context: Real CXL-HM prototype evaluation under two configurations: (1) single-aggregator serving, and (2) Prefill-Decode (PD) disaggregated serving with 64 GB per worker (256 GB total). Uses RDMA-capable network (ConnectX-6 RNIC, 100-200 Gbps) for remote memory access. Leverages vLLM serving engine with PagedAttention and Dynamo distributed framework with NIXL for P-D KV transfer. Models: Llama-3.1-8B (16 MB KV blocks) and Qwen2.5-32B (32 MB KV blocks) with FP16/BF16 KV cache and 128-token vLLM block size. Workloads: Dynamo AIPerf synthetic benchmark with mooncake trace, and LMSYS dataset for realistic multi-turn conversations. Setup: 4P-1D-1S (4 prefill, 1 decode, 1 scheduler) configuration.
facts.limitations: Evidence pack covers abstract/intro/background and limited evaluation sections; some implementation details remain in unread sections. The 3.0x and 1.45x performance improvement claims from abstract are not directly validated in visible sections - concrete TTFT measurements show HyMCache at 27.4s vs LMCache at 17.2s for Qwen2.5-32B E2E median TTFT (Turn 1-7). Cost estimates are FPGA prototype projections, not production ASIC pricing. RDMA network RTT and queue depth characteristics are not explicitly measured. The supplement provides specific Mooncake comparison (22.0s vs 27.4s TTFT, ~30% performance gap) but does not validate the abstract multiplier claims. CXL-HM internal cache management policies are not detailed in visible text.
facts.project_relevance: This source addresses KV-cache memory tiering for multi-turn LLM serving, which is highly relevant to cross-region cache sharing questions. The CXL-HM approach explores remote memory access over RDMA networks, which directly relates to WAN RTT and bandwidth considerations for KV cache transport. The 16x DRAM reduction versus 30% performance trade-off quantifies a key cost-performance decision point relevant to cross-region cache economics. Request-level prefix prefetching for predictable, append-only access patterns could inform compression and prefill strategies for cross-domain transfer. The measured NVMe-oF bandwidth degradation from 23 GB/s to 6.5 GB/s with filesystem overhead highlights software stack costs relevant to cross-domain transport. However, this paper focuses on intra-datacenter CXL/RDMA memory tiers rather than true WAN cross-region deployment; actual cross-region WAN latency (tens of ms) would be orders of magnitude higher than the CXL/RDMA latencies discussed. ConnectX-6 RNIC at 200 Gbps provides high-bandwidth intra-DC transport but does not represent WAN cross-region constraints.

evidence_gaps.question: What are the exact baseline LMCache configuration, workload characteristics (model, dataset, trace), and specific performance metrics (TTFT, TTFT, throughput, P99 latency) that support the 3.0x and 1.45x claims?
What are the actual RDMA network characteristics (RTT, bandwidth utilization, queue depths) and their impact on end-to-end serving latency?

facts.title: [AAFLOW+] Stateful Operator Abstraction with Zero-Copy Distributed KV Cache Orchestration for Multi-Agent Workflows
facts.event_hint: AAFLOW+: distributed KV cache orchestration system for multi-agent LLM workflows
facts.problem: Multi-agent LLM systems remain text-centric, requiring downstream agents to repeatedly recompute shared context through expensive prefill even when identical model state was already computed by upstream agents, causing increased TTFT, duplicated computation, and poor branch factor scalability for long-context workloads
facts.mechanism: Stateful operator abstraction extending AAFLOW from dataflow to stateflow, treating KV cache as a first-class distributed systems object with operators for materialization, transfer, fork, restricted composition, and eviction; runtime uses zero-copy communication, Arrow-based formats, explicit metadata, and transfer-aware scheduling to enable efficient KV state transfer between distributed components

evidence.claim: Stateful execution reduces TTFT by up to 50.2× at long context (from abstract; baseline and conditions not visible in current evidence)
evidence.condition: long context; baseline conditions not visible in current evidence

evidence.claim: On HF backend with Mistral at long context, AAFLOW+ reaches 0.041s mean TTFT vs 2.057s for AAFLOW-text, 2.017s for dense prefill, and 0.704s for KVCOMM; DistServe style remains at 0.123s
evidence.condition: HF backend; Mistral model; long context

evidence.claim: Stateful execution achieves 7.60× speedup at 16-agent scale for Mistral (AAFLOW+ 224.39s vs SGLang prefix 1704.86s; dense prefill 2716.11s)
Stateful execution achieves 7.63× speedup at 16-agent scale for Llama3 (AAFLOW+ 220.05s vs SGLang prefix 1679.81s)
Reduces peak KV memory by 1.72–6.10× and improves throughput by more than 7.74× (from abstract; workload and hardware conditions not visible in current evidence)
evidence.condition: workload and hardware conditions not visible in current evidence

facts.evaluation_context: GPU clusters; Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B models; multi-agent workflows (planner-retriever-solver, tree-of-thought, collaborative RAG); HF, vLLM, and SGLang backends; comparison against text-based agent communication; analytical cost model parameterized by empirical hardware microbenchmarks; trace-driven model to isolate KV-transfer limits
facts.limitations: Supplement provides partial experiment details (backends: HF, vLLM, SGLang; models: Mistral, Llama3) and specific TTFT/multi-agent latency comparisons, but key gaps remain: 50.2× TTFT, 1.72-6.10× memory, and 7.74× throughput claims lack visible baseline conditions and detailed configuration; specific network bandwidth thresholds for transfer vs recomputation decision not provided; network utilization, KVCache transmission volumes, and end-to-end P95 metrics not visible; synthetic deterministic prompts used with Y=64 output tokens; infrastructure assessments based on controlled experiments not production cluster data; scope focuses on shared-prefix multi-agent workflows not independent stateless inference; compatibility requires identical model architectures and positional encodings
facts.project_relevance: Directly addresses TPN questions about state-aware scheduling reducing TTFT/TPOT and KVCache transmission overhead; KV transfer over moderate-to-high bandwidth networks vs recomputation decision criterion (Equation 7) is network-aware; zero-copy distributed KV cache orchestration provides network-side mechanisms beyond pure GPU memory scheduling; project asks whether network perceives KVCache location and Token performance targets—AAFLOW+ makes KV placement and transfer explicit in distributed execution graph

evidence_gaps.question: What are the specific network bandwidth thresholds and transfer costs where KV transfer outperforms recomputation (cited as moderate-to-high bandwidth)?
What are the exact network utilization, KVCache transmission volumes, and end-to-end P95 metrics for the multi-agent workflows?

facts.title: KAP: Bridging the Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption Gap in LLM Systems
facts.event_hint: KAP paradigm introduction: Knowledge Access Planning for LLM serving with GraphSpec implementation
facts.problem: The Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption (KSRC) gap: LLM serving backends receive only serialized prompts, losing structured knowledge priors (ranked evidence, graph topology, multimodal alignment, confidence signals) from upstream selection processes. This forces uniform full-context KV consumption regardless of actual knowledge importance, increasing latency and degrading throughput as contexts lengthen.
facts.mechanism: Knowledge Access Planning (KAP) elevates structured knowledge priors to first-class execution artifacts through a universal intermediate representation (runtime access plan). The IR encodes selected knowledge units, runtime object mappings, logical positions, access policy, and verification policy. Instantiated as GraphSpec with Graph-RAG frontend and VLLM backend, using compiler-executor architecture to translate structured priors into KV access plans without altering model weights, training, or logical prompt semantics.

evidence.claim: GraphSpec reduces proposal-time KV access to 5.5% of source KV state at 128K context length while maintaining answer quality comparable to full-context decoding
evidence.condition: 128K-token long-context QA workload, proposal-time KV access metric

evidence.claim: GraphSpec achieves 1.19x decode-throughput speedup at 128K context length versus full-context decoding, with absolute performance of 51.70 TPS versus 45.68 TPS baseline at 64K context
Evaluated on four NVIDIA A800 80GB GPUs with tensor parallelism 4 and bfloat16 execution across 4K-128K long-context SPIQA QA workloads
Quality measured via SPIQA multimodal QA benchmark with LLM-as-judge metric achieving 87.9% pass rate versus 86.0% baseline and 95% human-audit agreement
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 12 Table 1, PDF Page 14 Table 4

evidence.claim: KAP decouples physical KV consumption from prompt length through GraphSpec compiler-executor architecture connecting Graph-RAG frontend to VLLM backend without altering model weights or training
evidence.baseline: linear physical cost growth with context length
evidence.condition: Theoretical phase-boundary model validation, Graph-RAG+VLLM instantiation

facts.evaluation_context: Long-context QA workloads spanning 4K to 128K token contexts. Knowledge-selection frontend uses Graph-RAG to produce structured priors (graph topology, ranked evidence). LLM serving backend uses VLLM v0.16.0 extended with GraphSpec. Hardware: four NVIDIA A800 80GB GPUs with tensor parallelism 4 and bfloat16 execution. Dataset: SPIQA multimodal QA benchmark grounded in scientific papers. Quality metric: LLM similarity with fact consistency (40%), information completeness (30%), logical structure (20%), expression quality (10%), validated by human audit with 95% agreement. Efficiency metrics: decode throughput (TPS), time-to-first-token (TTFT), retained-KV ratios. Batch size and concurrency settings not specified in supplement.
facts.limitations: Evaluation limited to long-context QA workloads on SPIQA dataset; generalization to other task types (code generation, multi-turn dialogue, agentic workflows) not addressed. Verification/fallback overhead not quantified. Phase-boundary model presented but positive-speedup regime conditions not fully specified. GraphSpec is one concrete instantiation; KAP paradigm generality claimed but only Graph-RAG+VLLM combination demonstrated. Batch size and concurrency configuration not specified, limiting reproducibility. TTFT includes plan compilation overhead but prefills are preserved for all methods.
facts.project_relevance: Directly addresses AI infra horizontal dynamics question: which systems/hardware changes affect end-to-end efficiency. KAP introduces execution-time planning layer between knowledge selection and LLM serving, reducing GPU memory bandwidth pressure and improving throughput for RAG systems. Hardware specifics now visible (A800 80GB, 4x TP=4, bfloat16) enabling infrastructure assessment. Absolute performance metrics (51.70 TPS vs 45.68 baseline, TTFT ~12.6s) provide concrete engineering boundaries. Quality validation via human audit (95% agreement) strengthens production relevance. Should be tracked as infra-level optimization paradigm; may warrant dedicated topic if adoption emerges in production serving stacks.
